edition.deck: A disputed election result, renewed conflict and questions of public accountability lead today’s coverage.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises consequential developments across the three sections, while grouping reporting on the same event and preserving what remains disputed or unconfirmed.

content.headline: Brazil’s presidential election heads to a run-off as Bolsonaro leads Lula
content.shortHeadline: Bolsonaro leads Lula as Brazil election goes to run-off
content.standfirst: Flávio Bolsonaro took 47% of the first-round vote to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s 45%, leaving Brazil’s presidential contest to be decided on 25 October. The result gives the right-wing challenger momentum, but the race is not over.

image.caption: Flávio Bolsonaro casts his vote at a polling station in Rio de Janeiro.

sources.originalTitle: Brazil election goes to run-off as right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro wins first round
Brazil’s presidential race goes to second round as Flávio Bolsonaro leads incumbent Lula
Brasiliens præsidentvalg skal afgøres i anden runde - en direkte duel mellem Bolsonaro og Lula

segments.body: With more than 99% of votes counted, Flávio Bolsonaro led incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, but neither reached the more than 50% needed to win outright. The two will face each other in a run-off on 25 October. Bolsonaro’s result was stronger than expected; votes from other right-wing candidates may help him, but the outcome remains uncertain.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s account also describes the right’s strong showing in legislative and state races, including 34 of 54 elected senators from the right or far right. That broader electoral strength will shape the political landscape whichever candidate wins the presidency.

segments.title: A contest over Brazil’s direction
segments.body: Bolsonaro, 45, is the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a failed coup. Flávio has pledged to seek amnesty for his father and supporters convicted over the January 2023 riots. Lula, 80, is seeking a fourth, non-consecutive term and has framed the choice as one about democracy. The campaign has also centred on crime, the economy and corruption.

content.headline: Russian drones strike Kyiv bridges as Germany pledges fresh support
content.shortHeadline: Russian drone hits Kyiv bridge during Merz’s visit
content.standfirst: A strike on Kyiv’s Northern Bridge injured two people and added to days of attacks on crossings over the Dnipro. Germany’s chancellor visited the city and agreed a new aid package, while traffic disruption and damage to infrastructure continue.

image.caption: A Russian drone strikes Kyiv’s Northern Bridge as vehicles cross it.

sources.originalTitle: Kyiv bridge hit in further Russian drone attack as German chancellor makes surprise visit

segments.body: A Russian drone struck Kyiv’s Northern Bridge on Sunday for the second day in a row, injuring two people, according to Mayor Vitali Klitschko. The Southern Bridge has also been hit during four consecutive days of attacks on the capital’s bridges. Both crossings remain standing, but damage and traffic restrictions have contributed to gridlock.

segments.title: Support and pressure on infrastructure
segments.body: The bridges carry heavy traffic between the two sides of the Dnipro River, and officials are considering temporary pontoon bridges and ferry services to keep the city connected. A separate strike damaged a heating main. During a visit to Kyiv, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz reaffirmed support for Ukraine; President Volodymyr Zelensky said a new package worth more than €1.3bn had been agreed, including weapons and energy-sector support.

content.headline: Yemen government declares offensive to retake Houthi-held territory
content.shortHeadline: Yemen government declares war to retake Houthi territory
content.standfirst: President Rashad al-Alimi says military operations will begin as fighting escalates between government forces and the Houthis. The group claims it attacked Saudi oil sites; Saudi Arabia has not commented on that claim.

image.caption: Soldiers travel near Taiz amid fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis.

sources.originalTitle: Yemen's government announces all-out war to reclaim land from Houthis

segments.body: Yemen’s internationally recognised government has announced an offensive to retake territory held by the Houthis. President Rashad al-Alimi said the aim was to extend state authority across the country. The announcement follows intensified fighting and reported Houthi gains along the Red Sea coast, including around the Bab al-Mandab shipping route.

segments.title: Claims of strikes and a worsening conflict
segments.body: The Houthis said they had attacked Saudi Aramco sites in Riyadh and the Khurais area, claiming the strikes caused large fires. Saudi Arabia has not commented on the latest claim; it has previously disputed Houthi accounts of attacks. The group also reportedly cut a key supply route between Taiz and Aden, potentially isolating Taiz. Yemen remains in a severe humanitarian crisis after years of war.

content.headline: Tigray rebels withdraw from Ethiopia’s regional capital as fighting nears
content.shortHeadline: TPLF forces withdraw from Tigray capital as fighting nears
content.standfirst: The Tigray People’s Liberation Front says it has temporarily left Mekelle to reduce risks to civilians. Residents told the BBC that pro-government forces now control the city, as renewed fighting raises fears of wider regional instability.

image.caption: A pro-government soldier stands guard on a street in Ethiopia’s Tigray region.

sources.originalTitle: Ethiopian rebel forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital

segments.body: The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) says it has temporarily withdrawn from Mekelle, the regional capital, as fighting with Ethiopia’s federal forces moves closer. Two residents told the BBC that pro-government forces now control the city; one said mobile phone services appeared to have resumed in parts of it.

segments.title: A fragile peace under strain
segments.body: Fighting has spread across parts of Tigray, Afar and Amhara, after months of worsening relations and accusations by both sides that the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement has been violated. The TPLF recently joined other armed movements in an alliance seeking to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government. Neighbouring Ethiopia and Eritrea have also severed diplomatic relations amid competing accusations of support for armed groups.

content.headline: Imran Khan supporters march towards Pakistan’s capital after talks fail
content.shortHeadline: Khan supporters march on Islamabad after talks collapse
content.standfirst: Thousands of supporters of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan are heading towards Islamabad after negotiations between his party and the government ended without agreement. His party is also demanding medical examination and treatment for Khan.

image.caption: Supporters march carrying flags of Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party.

sources.originalTitle: Supporters of jailed ex-PM Imran Khan march to Pakistan capital

segments.body: Supporters of Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party began marching from Lakki Marwat towards Islamabad on Sunday. The march had paused overnight and was expected to resume on Monday. Talks with the government ended in deadlock after the PTI said its request for access to Khan and for medical care had been rejected.

segments.title: Health concerns and political tensions
segments.body: Khan, 73, has been in prison since 2023 and faces more than 100 cases, which he says are politically motivated. His family says he has lost most of the vision in his right eye. Authorities have blocked routes into Islamabad with shipping containers. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi accused Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi of undermining negotiations; Afridi urged people to join the political movement.

content.headline: South Korean care-home director jailed for abusing disabled residents
content.shortHeadline: Care-home director jailed for abusing disabled residents
content.standfirst: A Seoul court sentenced the director of a state-subsidised care home to 15 years for sexually abusing two residents; a third charge resulted in a lesser conviction. The case has exposed concerns about safeguarding and how authorities hear disabled people’s accounts.

sources.originalTitle: Forced to call him 'Dad': Trial over sexual abuse in disabled care home shocks South Korea

segments.body: A court in Seoul sentenced the director of Saekdongwon, identified only by his surname Kim, to 15 years in prison for raping two residents with intellectual disabilities. He denies the allegations and is appealing. The court found a third resident’s account credible but convicted Kim of a lesser sexual-violence charge, saying it could not establish that force or threats had prevented her from resisting.

segments.title: Questions about investigation and care
segments.body: The BBC spoke to one of the women, whose name has been changed to protect her identity. A university assessment submitted as evidence found indications that at least 10 residents may have been abused, but the court did not address that finding. Activists say investigators relied too heavily on accounts from people able to describe events in complete sentences. The home has been ordered to close, but residents must first be relocated; plans for all 33 are still being developed.

content.headline: Six presumed dead after medical plane disappears off Massachusetts coast
content.shortHeadline: Six presumed dead after medical plane goes missing
content.standfirst: The US Coast Guard has ended its search for survivors after a medical transport aircraft disappeared on a flight from Bermuda to Boston. The operator says all six people aboard are presumed dead; the cause of the crash is not yet known.

image.caption: The medical transport aircraft was flying from Bermuda to Boston when it disappeared.

sources.originalTitle: All six passengers presumed dead after plane went missing off US coast

segments.body: A Gulfstream G-100 carrying four Canadian and two Bermudian nationals disappeared off the coast of Nantucket on Saturday. The US Coast Guard ended its search for survivors on Sunday, after authorities found a debris field from the aircraft. The operator, Latitude Air Ambulance, said the six people aboard are presumed to have died.

segments.title: Investigation underway
segments.body: The plane was carrying two pilots, two medical staff, a patient and the patient’s family escort from Bermuda to Boston. Flight data showed a steep drop in altitude before communications were lost; radio recordings indicate the pilot declared an emergency. Latitude said it would cooperate with authorities and cautioned that determining the cause of an aviation accident is a careful process.

content.headline: France to close up to 500 schools amid protests and clashes
content.shortHeadline: Up to 500 French schools to suspend lessons amid protests
content.standfirst: France’s education minister says lessons will be suspended in 400 to 500 high schools after violent clashes and damage to school buildings. Students are protesting shortages of teachers, crowded classrooms and deteriorating facilities.

image.caption: Riot police are deployed during student protests in France.

sources.originalTitle: France closes up to 500 schools Monday over student protests

segments.body: Between 400 and 500 high schools in France are expected to suspend lessons fully or partly on Monday because security conditions have not been met, Education Minister Édouard Geffray said. He said 24 schools had been burned or ransacked since protests began last week. The demonstrations have spread from Paris to other cities.

segments.title: Dispute over the protests’ direction
segments.body: Students have cited teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. Geffray blamed what he described as far-left activists for infiltrating the movement and engaging in violence; he said 78 education staff had been injured. Organisers have called for protests to continue on Tuesday, saying the government has not offered concrete measures. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu says the government is working on facilities, school schedules and university admissions.

content.headline: US withdraws bombers from RAF Fairford after security incident
content.shortHeadline: US pulls bombers from RAF Fairford after security incident
content.standfirst: All US bombers at the Gloucestershire base have returned to their home stations, after arrests linked to a suspected plot near the site. Washington has not given a reason for the withdrawal; British authorities have not commented.

image.caption: A US B-1 bomber takes off from RAF Fairford to return to the United States.

sources.originalTitle: US removes all bombers from RAF Fairford base
US bombers pulled from RAF Fairford base after suspected terror plot

segments.body: The US has withdrawn all its bombers from RAF Fairford, with a Pentagon official confirming they had been redeployed to their home stations. The aircraft are thought to include about a dozen B-1 bombers. The move follows a security incident near the base on 27 September, when police were alerted to three suspicious vehicles.

segments.title: What is known about the threat
segments.body: Six men were arrested during the investigation and later released on bail. Prime Minister Andy Burnham previously said there were strong indications Iran had played a part; Tehran denies involvement. The BBC says Whitehall sources have not disputed that the withdrawal was in response to the incident, describing it as an operational rather than political decision. The UK Ministry of Defence has not commented.

perspectives.body: The Guardian, citing US media and unnamed officials, reports that concerns intensified in the 24 hours before the withdrawal, though the nature of any new information has not been disclosed. That account differs in emphasis from the absence of a public US explanation.

content.headline: Thousands of child sexual offences reported at schools in England and Wales
content.shortHeadline: Police record thousands of sexual offences against children at schools
content.standfirst: Guardian analysis of police data found at least 8,500 reported sexual offences against children aged 12 and under on or near school premises between 2021 and 2025. The figures are incomplete and do not establish who committed every offence.

sources.originalTitle: Thousands of child-on-child sexual offences reported at schools in England and Wales
From unwanted touching to rape: the scale of child-on-child abuse in English and Welsh schools

segments.body: Police recorded at least 8,500 sexual offences against children aged 12 and under as occurring on or near schools in England and Wales from 2021 to 2025, an average of 4.7 reports a day, according to Guardian analysis. The data included almost 2,000 reports of rape or attempted rape. In at least 1,890 offences, the alleged perpetrator was described as under 18.

segments.title: The limits of the data and calls for action
segments.body: The analysis used responses from 33 of 43 police forces and may not capture the full scale of abuse; recording practices also vary. Most reports did not specify the alleged perpetrator’s age. The children’s commissioner for England described peer-on-peer abuse as widespread and too often brushed aside. Police leaders say the figures underline the need for prevention and safeguarding, while noting that increased awareness may also have helped victims report abuse.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s companion reporting adds interviews with lawyers and families about how schools respond after disclosures, including cases where children were left without adequate support. It also describes the difficulty of investigating allegations involving younger children below the age of criminal responsibility.

content.headline: Green Party adopts policy equating Zionism with racism, prompting dispute
content.shortHeadline: Greens adopt Zionism policy amid dispute over antisemitism and rights
content.standfirst: Members voted 1,022 to 813 for a motion describing Zionism as a form of racism and calling for a single Palestinian state. Most Green MPs opposed it, while Jewish members and legal experts have raised concerns about its consequences.

image.caption: Israeli flags at a pro-Israel rally outside the Green Party conference in Brighton.

sources.originalTitle: Green party votes to adopt policy that equates Zionism with racism

segments.body: The Green Party in England and Wales adopted a policy motion describing Zionism as a form of racism and calling for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state with equal rights for all. Four of the party’s five MPs opposed the motion. Party leader Zack Polanski missed the conference vote while campaigning in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election.

segments.title: Dispute over the motion’s implications
segments.body: Israel’s foreign ministry called the resolution antisemitic, saying it denies Jewish people self-determination. The Movement for Progressive Judaism also condemned it. Some Jewish Green members fear the policy could affect their participation in Jewish organisations; the motion does not explicitly require members to renounce Zionism, but an amendment against disciplining members over community affiliations was rejected. Some members are consulting lawyers, and a barrister cited in the report said the motion may risk breaching the Equality Act. The party says it will not tolerate discrimination or harassment.

content.headline: Experts warn UK lacks a plan to protect food supplies in a crisis
content.shortHeadline: Experts warn Britain is unprepared for a food supply crisis
content.standfirst: More than 150 experts say the UK’s reliance on imports and just-in-time deliveries leaves it exposed to climate shocks, cyberattacks and geopolitical disruption. They are urging ministers to build a national resilience plan and food storage capacity.

sources.originalTitle: British government ‘complacent about food as a national security matter’

segments.body: An open letter to Andy Burnham, signed by more than 150 academics, business leaders and community groups, warns that Britain has no plan for feeding people in a crisis. The signatories say the food system is import-dependent, holds little stock and is vulnerable to climate events, geopolitical shocks, cyberattacks and energy outages.

segments.title: Proposals and household preparedness
segments.body: The letter calls for local food resilience committees, an audit of reliance on imports and large suppliers, and food storage at national and community levels. It also argues that advice for households to stock up may overlook people who cannot afford to do so. The Cabinet Office is preparing a campaign encouraging households to keep emergency supplies; ministers have not announced a national food-storage plan.

content.headline: North Sea strike threat could disrupt UK fuel supplies, Unite warns
content.shortHeadline: North Sea strike threat raises risk to UK fuel supplies
content.standfirst: More than 160 Apache offshore workers have backed strike action over pay, Unite says. The union warns disruption could affect the Forties pipeline; Apache says it has contingency plans and does not expect other producers to be affected.

image.caption: The Forties Bravo oil platform in the North Sea.

sources.originalTitle: Strikes by North Sea oil workers could ‘severely disrupt’ UK fuel supplies

segments.body: Unite says more than 160 Apache offshore workers have voted for industrial action after pay talks broke down. Strikes could begin later this month and affect the Forties and Beryl fields. The union warns disruption at a key platform could put pressure on the Forties pipeline system, which it says handles almost a third of UK oil and gas.

segments.title: The company disputes the scale of the risk
segments.body: Apache says it offered a 4% pay rise and described its offer as fair, adding that it has plans to maintain safe operations during any action. The company says it does not expect a strike to affect other producers. Unite argues that the offer would amount to a real-terms cut for many workers. The strike threat comes as consumers face high fuel prices, but its eventual effect on supplies is not known.

content.headline: AI-generated child sexual abuse images exceed last year’s total, watchdog says
content.shortHeadline: AI child abuse images already exceed last year’s total
content.standfirst: The Internet Watch Foundation says it assessed 6,310 AI-generated images that met the legal definition of child sexual abuse in the first half of 2026—40% more than its total for all of 2025. It is calling for binding rules on AI developers.

sources.originalTitle: Internet Watch Foundation reports huge rise in AI child sexual abuse material

segments.body: The Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) says it assessed 6,310 AI-generated images meeting the legal definition of child sexual abuse in the first half of 2026. That is 40% more than the total it assessed in 2025. The figures concern still images; the IWF says AI-generated videos have also risen, but they are not included in this comparison.

segments.title: Calls for safer technology
segments.body: The IWF is urging binding legislation to require companies to build safer AI models. The government says AI-generated child sexual abuse material is illegal and that it has also banned adapting or distributing models intended to create it. A service that helps remove intimate images has received 420 reports from children about images they believed had been faked or manipulated, already above its 2025 total.

content.headline: BBC cuts leave staff uncertain as wider channel changes are reported
content.shortHeadline: BBC job cuts fuel fears of further losses and channel closures
content.standfirst: The BBC is seeking to save £500m, with staff reporting low morale as job reductions are announced in stages. Reports of possible channel closures and a wider shift online remain unconfirmed by the corporation.

sources.originalTitle: BBC morale dented by gradual ‘bloodletting’ after weeks of job cuts
BBC begins move towards online-only TV – these channels and shows are at risk

segments.body: The BBC’s savings plan aims to cut £500m and could involve up to 2,000 jobs, according to Guardian reporting. Staff say the staggered announcements have damaged morale and fear further cuts. Redundancies have been announced across areas including news, local radio and technology; the corporation is also reviewing redundancy terms.

segments.title: Possible changes to services
segments.body: The Guardian reports that BBC Scotland and BBC Three may become online-only, while the i Paper describes wider possibilities affecting other television and radio services over time. The BBC has not confirmed those reported closures and says it does not comment on speculation. The financial pressure comes as viewing habits move towards streaming, but the future shape of specific channels remains unsettled.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s report details the wider strategic possibility of shifting more services towards iPlayer and Sounds, while also noting that several channel options remain under discussion rather than announced decisions.

content.headline: Housing associations receiving grants face scrutiny over tenant conditions
content.shortHeadline: Housing landlords winning grants face questions over poor conditions
content.standfirst: An investigation found six housing associations awarded public grants for new homes each had more than 100 maladministration findings from the Housing Ombudsman last year. The findings vary in severity, and providers say they are working to improve services.

image.caption: A home with reported mould and rodent problems, among the conditions raised in the investigation.

sources.originalTitle: Landlords of damp, mice-infested houses are building Burnham’s new homes

segments.body: Six housing associations selected for public funding to build homes each had more than 100 maladministration findings in the previous year, according to an i Paper review of Housing Ombudsman data. The organisations are among 33 providers sharing £9.5bn under the Social and Affordable Housing Programme. Ombudsman findings include cases where service failures negatively affected residents.

segments.title: Repair records and competing pressures
segments.body: The report describes complaints involving damp, mould, pests and delays to repairs, including cases involving Clarion, Sanctuary and Hyde. Providers contacted by the i Paper said they take complaints seriously, have invested in repairs or have acted on ombudsman findings; several disputed aspects of the reporting or declined to comment. Housing experts argue that grants for building new homes should be matched by stronger attention to existing tenants’ conditions.

content.headline: Unauthorised access exposed personal data of 8.8 million people in Denmark
content.shortHeadline: CPR access breach exposed data on 8.8 million people
content.standfirst: Authorities say an unauthorised party misused a company’s legitimate access to Denmark’s Civil Registration System to obtain names, addresses and CPR numbers. The full scope of the incident is still being assessed.

sources.originalTitle: Uvedkommende har haft adgang til 8,8 millioner CPR-numre

segments.body: The Danish Civil Registration System (CPR) says an unauthorised party obtained access to personal information on about 8.8 million registered people by misusing a Danish company’s legitimate search access. The data included names, addresses and CPR numbers. Names and addresses of people with protected address status were not included in the access, according to the initial review.

segments.title: Investigation and advice to the public
segments.body: The company’s access has been stopped and the incident reported to the Danish Data Protection Agency. The Ministry of Research, Education and Digital Affairs says authorities are working to establish the full scope and have started measures intended to prevent a similar incident. Minister Christina Egelund urged people to stay alert and consult sikkerdigital.dk.

content.headline: Police acknowledge failure to update caller before woman’s fatal overdose
content.shortHeadline: Police change procedures after fatal case and missed dispatch
content.standfirst: Fyn Police say they should have told a caller they would not attend a disturbance report before a 23-year-old woman was found dead. Experts told DR she would likely have survived if she had reached hospital, but the police say the original call did not indicate an urgent emergency.

sources.originalTitle: Nabo ringede forgæves: Politiet erkender fejl i sag om 23-årigs død

segments.body: A neighbour called police twice after hearing banging and groaning from the flat of 23-year-old Cecilie Voller Kjærulff in Odense. Officers did not attend, and she was found dead the next day. An autopsy concluded she probably died from an overdose of medication prescribed for bipolar disorder, with alcohol and other drugs also detected in her blood.

segments.title: Police response and what remains unknown
segments.body: Fyn Police acknowledge they should have informed the caller that a patrol would not be sent after all. The force says its assessment at the time—that the call was not an urgent police matter—was not itself an error, while recognising that more information might have changed the response. Experts consulted by DR said she would likely have survived if she had reached hospital when the neighbour called. The force has changed call-handling procedures; the family remains critical of its response.

content.headline: Three Danish governing parties urge citizenship bill for 2,055 applicants
content.shortHeadline: Coalition parties demand action on 2,055 citizenship cases
content.standfirst: The Moderates, Socialist People’s Party and Social Liberals want 2,055 applicants who met citizenship criteria to receive a decision without waiting for a review of proposed screening. The government has paused the cases following an election.

image.caption: Minister Morten Bødskov faces pressure from coalition partners over paused citizenship applications.

sources.originalTitle: Tre regeringspartier går imod regeringens egen indfødsretspolitik

segments.body: Three parties in Denmark’s governing coalition—Moderates, Socialist People’s Party and Social Liberals—are urging the government to revive a citizenship bill covering 2,055 people. Their names had been included in a bill awaiting formal approval, but the cases were put on hold after an election while an expert group considers screening applicants for anti-democratic attitudes.

segments.title: Concerns about the pause
segments.body: The parties say applicants who met the existing criteria should not be left in uncertainty while the review proceeds. A researcher at the Danish Institute for Human Rights told DR that pausing cases involving 72 stateless children born in Denmark may conflict with obligations to prevent statelessness. The government’s citizenship minister has said he expects the expert group’s report by the end of the year; the Social Democrats defend waiting for its findings.

content.headline: Divorce case delays can affect where children live, Danish lawyers warn
content.shortHeadline: Long family-court delays may shape where children live
content.standfirst: A father waited 578 days for a final decision on where his children should live. Family lawyers warn that delay can reshape children’s routines and influence later rulings; the children’s mother says the case is more complex than his account suggests.

image.caption: In one reported case, a final decision on where children would live took 578 days.

sources.originalTitle: Ventetid i skilsmissesager kan bestemme, om barnet bor hos mor eller far

segments.body: It took 578 days for a final court decision in Ragnar Dixen’s dispute over where his children should live after a divorce. During the process, he saw them for only a few hours a week. A district court initially ruled they should live with him, but after an appeal the High Court decided they should primarily live with their mother, who had been their main carer since the separation.

segments.title: Concern over delay and fairness
segments.body: The chair of Danish Family Lawyers says long processing times can influence outcomes because children may become settled with one parent while a case is pending. A judge agrees that circumstances can change, but says it is impossible to know whether decisions would have differed with shorter waits. The children’s mother told DR she agrees the delay did not help the conflict, but says the case is not as simple as Dixen describes and the final ruling was not based on delay alone.

content.headline: Denmark to widen busy Copenhagen ring road and cut speed limit
content.shortHeadline: Copenhagen ring road to gain a lane as speed limit falls
content.standfirst: The 17-kilometre Motorring 3 is to be widened from three lanes to four across most of its route, with noise-reducing asphalt and a lower speed limit. Work is scheduled to begin in 2027 and finish in 2029 or 2030.

image.caption: The plan would widen most of the Motorring 3 around Copenhagen from three lanes to four.

sources.originalTitle: En af Danmarks mest trafikerede motorveje skal nu udvides

segments.body: The political parties behind Denmark’s Infrastructure Plan 2035 have agreed to widen most of the Motorring 3 around Copenhagen from three lanes to four. The 17-kilometre road carries more than 145,000 vehicles a day. The speed limit will fall from 110 to 90 kilometres per hour, and noise-reducing asphalt is planned.

segments.title: Noise impact and timetable
segments.body: The Danish Road Directorate estimates the asphalt could reduce noise by three to four decibels for about 40% of homes alongside the road. Gladsaxe’s mayor welcomed the noise measures but said local leaders would have preferred an 80-kilometre-per-hour limit. The work is expected to start in 2027 and be completed between 2029 and 2030.

content.headline: Danish investment fund faces US lawsuit alleging business misconduct
content.shortHeadline: Waterland denies allegations in US lawsuit over concert business
content.standfirst: A US company alleges that Danish-Dutch private equity firm Waterland and two Danish employees misused confidential business information and sought to damage its business. Waterland denies wrongdoing and has asked a judge to dismiss the case.

sources.originalTitle: Interne mails, kristen musik og voldtægtsbeskyldninger: Dansk kapitalfond beskyldes for at ville 'knuse' konkurrent

segments.body: Thriving Children Advocates (TCA), which arranges sponsorships for Christian concert tours, alleges that Waterland and two Danish employees used confidential information obtained during takeover talks to build a competing business. The allegations are part of a US lawsuit involving more than 30 defendants. The claims have not been established in court.

segments.title: Waterland rejects the claims
segments.body: Waterland and the two employees deny the allegations and argue that the case should be dismissed, describing it as an unsupported attempt by a former market leader to fight competition. The lawsuit also alleges a coordinated effort to damage TCA through reporting about a singer’s alleged misconduct; the defendants reject that claim as well. A judge must decide whether the case proceeds.

content.headline: Danish households may have to accept adverts to receive local newspapers
content.shortHeadline: Local paper delivery linked to advertising in postboxes
content.standfirst: FK Distribution says it cannot afford to deliver some local newspapers without also distributing adverts. Readers can opt out of both, while a regional media company fears losing newspaper subscribers and advertising reach.

image.caption: Households may receive advertising leaflets along with local newspapers, or opt out of both.

sources.originalTitle: Hvis du vil have lokalavisen, er du nu også tvunget til at få reklamer i postkassen

segments.body: From 1 November, households receiving many local newspapers through FK Distribution will have to accept a selection of advertising leaflets or stop delivery of the papers as well. The company says delivering local papers alone is too costly under current market conditions. If households do not choose specific adverts, they will receive a standard package.

segments.title: Reader and publisher concerns
segments.body: Some Aalborg residents say they may give up their local paper rather than receive unwanted adverts. Det Nordjyske Mediehus says it is unhappy with the change and fears losing readers and advertisers. FK Distribution says households have been notified and can change their choices or opt out of the combined delivery altogether.

content.headline: Pandora opens major Vietnam factory beside Lego’s plant
content.shortHeadline: Pandora opens Vietnam factory as Danish firms expand production
content.standfirst: Pandora’s new factory near Ho Chi Minh City cost about 1 billion Danish kroner and is expected to produce up to 60 million pieces of jewellery a year. The company says it could employ 7,000 people when fully operational.

image.caption: Pandora and Lego executives at the opening of Pandora’s new factory in Vietnam.

sources.originalTitle: Millioner Milliarder: To danske topdirektører er blevet naboer på den anden side af Jorden

segments.body: Danish jewellery company Pandora has opened a factory on the outskirts of Ho Chi Minh City, its first outside Thailand. The site cost about 1 billion Danish kroner and is designed to produce up to 60 million pieces of jewellery annually once fully operational, increasing Pandora’s global production capacity by 50%, according to the report.

segments.title: A growing manufacturing hub
segments.body: The factory is expected to employ 7,000 people when fully operational and sits beside one of Lego’s global factories. The neighbouring Danish investments reflect Vietnam’s appeal as a manufacturing location, the report says. The factory’s stated capacity and employment figures refer to its future full operation, not necessarily its current output or staffing.

content.headline: Elfyn Evans wins first British WRC title in 25 years after Solberg crash
content.shortHeadline: Evans wins first British WRC title in 25 years
content.standfirst: The Welsh driver secured the 2026 championship when Oliver Solberg crashed near the end of the final stage in Sardinia. Evans, a five-time runner-up, finished five points clear.

image.caption: Elfyn Evans, the 2026 World Rally Championship winner.

sources.originalTitle: Evans ends Britain's 25-year wait for WRC champion

segments.body: Elfyn Evans and co-driver Scott Martin are world rally champions after a dramatic finish to the season in Italy. Evans had a 21-point lead before the final round, but that advantage had dwindled to one point going into the last of 17 stages.

segments.title: A dramatic finish
segments.body: Oliver Solberg needed to beat his Toyota team-mate on the final stage to take the title. He was closing on Evans with only a few hundred metres left when he crashed; he finished the stage nine seconds behind Evans and five points short in the championship.

content.headline: England thrash Croatia 7-0 as Modric calls defeat 'catastrophic'
content.shortHeadline: England rout Croatia 7-0; Modric calls it catastrophic
content.standfirst: England recorded Croatia's heaviest defeat as Luka Modric said he felt ashamed of the performance. Jude Bellingham scored and supplied three assists in a dominant Nations League win.

image.caption: Croatia captain Luka Modric, whose side lost 7-0 to England.

sources.originalTitle: Modric 'ashamed' of Croatia's 'catastrophic night'
Bellingham unlocks new level and potential to be 'one of the greatest'

segments.body: England beat Croatia 7-0 in Rijeka, scoring five times before Modric was substituted in the 57th minute. Harry Kane and Bukayo Saka each scored twice, with Jude Bellingham, Anthony Gordon and Morgan Rogers also on the scoresheet.

segments.title: Bellingham's influence
segments.body: Bellingham scored and registered three assists, the first England player to record three in a game since Trent Alexander-Arnold against San Marino in 2021. He also wore the captain's armband after Kane went off.

perspectives.body: Roy Keane praised Bellingham's running power, goal threat and work off the ball, saying he could become one of the greatest players of all time. England manager Thomas Tuchel said the midfielder was still developing.

segments.title: Modric's verdict
segments.body: Modric described the performance as a "catastrophic night" and said that, in 20 years as an international, it was the first time he had felt ashamed after a game. Croatia are third in Group A3 and face Spain next.

content.headline: Roosters edge Knights 19-18 to win NRL Grand Final
content.shortHeadline: Roosters win NRL final 19-18 in Nawaqanitawase's last game
content.standfirst: Mark Nawaqanitawase scored twice as Sydney held off Newcastle for a 16th title. The dual-code winger is leaving rugby league after the final, close to a possible return to union.

image.caption: Mark Nawaqanitawase, who scored twice in the NRL Grand Final.

sources.originalTitle: Dual-code winger Nawaqanitawase stars as Roosters win NRL Final

segments.body: Sydney Roosters beat Newcastle Knights 19-18 in the NRL Grand Final, holding on after Greg Marzhew scored late to bring Newcastle within a point. It is the Roosters' first title since 2019 and their 16th overall.

segments.title: A final flourish
segments.body: Mark Nawaqanitawase crossed in each half in his last match before leaving rugby league. He switched from union to the Roosters in 2024 and could represent Australia at next year's rugby union World Cup. Newcastle had been seeking their first title since 2001.

content.headline: Wu Yize wins Shenzhen Open and rises to world number two
content.shortHeadline: Wu wins Shenzhen Open to move up to world number two
content.standfirst: The world champion beat Yuan Sijun 10-5 for his first ranking title since winning at the Crucible. His rise puts China’s players first and second in the world rankings for the first time.

image.caption: Wu Yize, winner of the Shenzhen Open.

sources.originalTitle: Wu wins first title since Crucible at Shenzhen Open

segments.body: Wu Yize beat fellow Chinese player Yuan Sijun 10-5 in the Shenzhen Open final, earning the £177,000 top prize. The 22-year-old moves to a career-high second in the rankings, behind Zhao Xintong.

segments.title: A strong week
segments.body: After beating Judd Trump 6-1 in the semi-finals, Wu took a 3-1 lead in the final. Yuan won three frames in a row, but Wu led 5-4 after the opening session and pulled away with breaks of 74 and 62 in the evening.

content.headline: Wales lose to Denmark as Bellamy criticises four-game international window
content.shortHeadline: Bellamy says four-game window disadvantages Wales
content.standfirst: A Rasmus Hojlund penalty gave Denmark a 1-0 win in Cardiff, leaving Wales with three points from four Nations League games. Craig Bellamy says the expanded international break puts smaller squads under strain.

image.caption: Wales manager Craig Bellamy, whose side lost 1-0 to Denmark.

sources.originalTitle: Bellamy bemoans new schedule after Denmark loss

segments.body: Wales were beaten 1-0 by Denmark, with Rasmus Hojlund scoring a 75th-minute penalty. Goalkeeper Danny Ward had made two important saves before his error and foul led to the decisive spot-kick. Wales have three points from four games.

segments.title: Bellamy's concern over workload
segments.body: Bellamy said the four-match international window was a disadvantage for Wales, especially with injuries affecting his squad. He said the schedule puts smaller nations under stress because they lack the depth to rotate players as readily as bigger teams. Wales climbed to third in Group A4 on their head-to-head record against Norway.

content.headline: Ireland coach says Israel tried to intimidate his side amid spitting allegations
content.shortHeadline: Ireland-Israel tensions continue amid spitting allegations
content.standfirst: Heimir Hallgrimsson said he felt Israel were trying to intimidate Ireland during their 1-1 Nations League draw. An alleged spitting incident at half-time has not been established, and Israel's coach said he saw nothing.

image.caption: Players from the Republic of Ireland and Israel clash at half-time.

sources.originalTitle: Israel 'tried to intimidate' Irish amid spitting row - Hallgrimsson

segments.body: The Republic of Ireland and Israel drew 1-1 in a tense Nations League match played behind closed doors in Serbia. The teams clashed at half-time. Ireland coach Heimir Hallgrimsson said he felt Israel had tried to intimidate his players, but said he did not see the alleged spitting incident.

segments.title: The allegation and wider tensions
segments.body: The Irish Times reported an allegation by Ireland head of athletic performance Damien Doyle that an Israel player spat at him. Israel coach Ran Ben-Shimon said he was in the dressing room at half-time and saw nothing; he said he would check what happened. The report also notes a separate FAI investigation into whether Ireland forward Adam Idah was racially abused by Israel fans during the teams' earlier meeting.

content.headline: Arsenal fall 10 points behind WSL leaders after 4-2 loss to Manchester City
content.shortHeadline: Arsenal 10 points off WSL leaders after City defeat
content.standfirst: Arsenal's poor start continued as Manchester City came from behind twice to win 4-2. Renee Slegers says the club remains aligned behind her, while planning a review during the international break.

image.caption: Arsenal manager Renee Slegers, who led the club to the 2025 Women's Champions League title.

sources.originalTitle: Arsenal 10 points off WSL leaders - is Slegers' job at risk?

segments.body: Arsenal have won two of their opening seven matches in all competitions and sit 10th in the WSL, 10 points behind leaders Manchester City. Sunday's 4-2 defeat at City was their fourth league game without a win; Alessia Russo's goal was her first in the WSL this season.

segments.title: Pressure and a planned review
segments.body: Slegers said she was not worried about her position and remained energised, while acknowledging that results had been disappointing. Sources at the club said she retained their full backing. She plans a review of the season so far during the international break, as Arsenal look to address another slow start.

content.headline: Sabalenka stunned at China Open as Djokovic fights into the semi-finals
content.shortHeadline: Sabalenka stunned; Djokovic reaches China Open semis
content.standfirst: Nikola Bartunkova beat Aryna Sabalenka in straight sets, a day after Elena Rybakina's exit. Novak Djokovic came from a set down to beat Alexander Zverev and reach the men's last four.

image.caption: Aryna Sabalenka, beaten by Nikola Bartunkova at the China Open.

sources.originalTitle: Sabalenka stunned by Bartunkova at China Open
Djokovic beats Zverev to reach China Open semis

segments.body: World number two Aryna Sabalenka lost 6-4 6-3 to 34th-ranked Nikola Bartunkova at the China Open. The upset came a day after top seed Elena Rybakina was knocked out by Alina Charaeva, marking the first time since 2015 that the women's tournament's top two seeds failed to reach the round of 16.

segments.title: Djokovic advances
segments.body: Novak Djokovic recovered from a set down to beat world number two Alexander Zverev 4-6 6-4 6-4 and reach the men's semi-finals. He has won all 32 of his matches in Beijing and is still seeking his first title of 2026.

content.headline: Grouper’s Liz Harris finds wary hope in collaboration after a streaming scam
content.shortHeadline: Grouper’s Liz Harris on collaboration, virality and scam artists
content.standfirst: A viral afterlife for an old song brought new listeners and a royalty scam; reforming dream-pop trio Helen, meanwhile, reminded the elusive artist of the restorative power of making music with friends.

image.caption: Liz Harris of Grouper and Helen.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trio

segments.body: Liz Harris has built Grouper’s intimate, elusive music while keeping the music industry at arm’s length. Then “Poison Tree,” a song she wrote in her twenties, took off online. Harris says someone had fraudulently registered and uploaded it, earning around six figures before she and her label shut down the scam and recovered what she was owed.

segments.title: A different kind of company
segments.body: The experience deepened Harris’s wariness of streaming platforms, where she says fake remixes and tracks with matching titles can be used to siphon royalties. But working again with her friends in Helen has offered a counterweight: the trio’s new album, Linda’s Head, brought her a welcome sense of shared purpose and, she says, was restorative during a difficult period.

content.headline: Erasure’s Andy Bell and Vince Clarke lean on four decades of friendship
content.shortHeadline: Erasure’s Andy Bell and Vince Clarke on friendship and grief
content.standfirst: Their 20th album arrives after a painful period for both bandmates, while Clarke steps away from touring following his wife’s death. Their conversation reveals the history and affection behind that decision.

image.caption: Vince Clarke and Andy Bell of Erasure.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s a deep soul connection’: Erasure on how 40 years of friendship got them through grief – and why Vince Clarke has quit touring

segments.body: Andy Bell and Vince Clarke say their long friendship helped them through bereavement: Clarke’s wife, Tracy Hurley Martin, died in 2024, and Bell’s partner, Paul Hickey, died in 2012. Clarke credits Bell with giving him the support he needed. Their closeness also shapes the new Erasure album, Radio!! Radio!!, which Bell describes as a call for calmer times.

segments.title: A changed tour
segments.body: For the first time in Erasure’s history, Clarke will not perform on the band’s coming arena tour. He will serve remotely as musical director, with keyboard technician Howard Rider playing the parts on stage. Asked whether his wife’s death is the main reason, Clarke answers yes. Bell says the arrangement will not feel the same without his trusted partner beside him.

content.headline: Interpol’s new album brings fresh angles to the band’s familiar sound
content.shortHeadline: Interpol find new angles on This Mirror Weighs a Ton
content.standfirst: The band’s eighth album keeps its angular indie-rock identity but brings in new collaborators, a return to recording in New York and more varied arrangements. Its founders also challenge the rosy mythology of the early-2000s scene.

image.caption: Interpol founders Paul Banks and Daniel Kessler.

sources.originalTitle: Interpol: ‘People romanticise the Noughties music scene. We weren’t all friends’

segments.body: Interpol’s This Mirror Weighs a Ton is presented as a return to form, but the changes are part of the point. The band tried an outside producer, Andrew Wyatt, brought touring bassist Brad Truax into the writing process and recorded in New York for the first time since 2014. The result ranges from tense guitar-led songs to piano ballads and the band’s first use of acoustic guitar.

segments.title: A less romantic scene
segments.body: Founders Paul Banks and Daniel Kessler also push back on the idea that the early-2000s New York music scene was one big community of friends. They recall sharing clubs and a moment in time, but say the popular image of bands lending one another instruments and moving as a united circle did not match their experience.

content.headline: Venom’s Cronos brought punk’s unruly spirit to heavy metal
content.shortHeadline: Cronos made Venom’s metal raw, unruly and influential
content.standfirst: As frontman of Venom, Conrad “Cronos” Lant helped give black metal its name and pushed heavy music towards a rougher, more confrontational sound. His ferocious stage persona was only one part of a long career.

image.caption: Venom frontman Cronos performing in 1985.

sources.originalTitle: No one could terrify like Cronos, the black metal innovator who reignited rock’s hellraising attitude

segments.body: When Venom emerged from Newcastle in the late 1970s, Cronos thought metal had gone soft. The band answered with a DIY attack: hoarse vocals, hammering riffs and lyrics that made occult imagery deliberately confrontational. Venom’s 1982 album Black Metal gave a name to a subgenre, while Cronos’s snarling stage presence became a model for generations of metal frontmen.

segments.title: Beyond the stage persona
segments.body: The persona did not tell the whole story. Cronos left Venom for several years, trained as a fitness instructor and enjoyed birdwatching; he later returned to lead the band through more personnel changes. He also rejected the violence associated with some later black-metal acts, lamenting that they were known for it rather than their music.

content.headline: Soft Cell’s final album became a farewell after Dave Ball’s death
content.shortHeadline: Marc Almond on Soft Cell’s final album and Dave Ball
content.standfirst: Marc Almond and Dave Ball had finished Danceteria together just two days before Ball died in 2025. Almond recalls their friendship and the New York nightlife that shaped the album’s bittersweet farewell.

image.caption: Marc Almond and Dave Ball of Soft Cell.

sources.originalTitle: Soft Cell’s Marc Almond: ‘We finished the album – two days later Dave passed away’

segments.body: Soft Cell had agreed that their new songs were finished when Dave Ball died, two days later, in October 2025. For Marc Almond, that makes Danceteria the duo’s sixth and final album: he says he would not make another Soft Cell record without Ball. The album looks back to the pair’s early-1980s experiences in New York, both its exuberant clubs and its loneliness.

segments.title: A bond beyond the music
segments.body: Almond describes a friendship that survived nearly five decades without a serious falling-out. He is relieved they completed the record together, and remembers Ball as happy with it. Their recollections also follow the changing gay nightlife they knew: the freedom of the city’s underground clubs, followed by fear and loss as AIDS devastated the scene.

content.headline: Lulu returns to recording with new freedom after confronting addiction
content.shortHeadline: Lulu’s return to music comes with hard-won freedom
content.standfirst: The singer’s first new album in years is also a chance to set her own direction. She reflects on sobriety, the pressures that shaped her early career and the music that has repeatedly helped her begin again.

image.caption: Singer Lulu, whose new album marks a return to recording.

sources.originalTitle: Lulu: ‘I’m not proud of being an alcoholic – but I’m not ashamed’

segments.body: Lulu says writing about her past in her memoir was difficult but cathartic. She has spoken publicly about a long-hidden alcohol addiction and getting sober in 2013. “I’m not proud of it, but I’m not ashamed,” she says, describing the relief of no longer keeping that part of her life secret.

segments.title: A voice of her own
segments.body: Her new album, Let the Girl Sing Out, is being made with her brother Billy Lawrie, with Lulu co-writing and setting the artistic direction. She says that autonomy is what she wanted throughout a career in which others often steered her towards material that did not feel like her. Music, she says, has repeatedly opened a new beginning.

content.headline: Elvis Costello’s debut comes into focus in a sprawling anniversary set
content.shortHeadline: A 104-track set reveals the making of Elvis Costello’s debut
content.standfirst: Pitchfork’s review finds the five-disc edition of My Aim Is True valuable not just as a trove for collectors, but as a portrait of a young songwriter gradually finding his voice and musical identity.

image.caption: Elvis Costello, whose debut album is revisited in a new anniversary edition.

sources.originalTitle: My Aim Is True (49th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: The new 104-track edition follows Elvis Costello from earlier demos and recordings with Flip City to the songs and performances surrounding My Aim Is True. Pitchfork argues that the material makes the apparent leap of his debut feel less sudden: Costello was already a skilled songwriter, still trying out influences and approaches before punk-era urgency sharpened his persona.

segments.title: A complicated legacy
segments.body: The review sees the box set as a rare reissue that earns its scale. Demos and live recordings add context, while the finished album retains the wit, anger and tightly wound songwriting that made it a landmark. The later discs are less essential, but the collection’s arc gives fans a clearer view of how Declan MacManus became Elvis Costello.

content.headline: The Beatles’ Rubber Soul remains in motion in an expansive new edition
content.shortHeadline: Rubber Soul’s many versions come alive in a new box set
content.standfirst: The deluxe edition collects UK and US versions, stereo and mono mixes, outtakes and a new remix. Pitchfork’s review argues that the album’s history is less a single definitive object than a record shaped by creative choices and commerce.

sources.originalTitle: Rubber Soul (Super Deluxe)

segments.body: Rubber Soul marked a turning point for the Beatles and for pop, as the band joined self-written songs and adventurous arrangements to mass appeal. The new edition gathers its UK and US releases, mono and stereo mixes, outtakes and a new mix, letting listeners hear how recording decisions and the American track list produced different versions of the album.

segments.title: No single definitive version
segments.body: Pitchfork’s review finds the outtakes especially revealing: they show the band working quickly under pressure rather than simply fulfilling a story of inevitable greatness. Its central argument is that no one mix can settle the album’s meaning; each version brings a different balance of intimacy, punch and detail, and listeners arrive with their own preferred Rubber Soul.

content.headline: John Cena’s Hollywood career tests the limits of loyalty
content.shortHeadline: John Cena on Hollywood, WWE and the cost of loyalty
content.standfirst: The wrestler-turned-actor discusses his comic screen persona and his loyalty to WWE, including his continued friendship with former boss Vince McMahon, who denies allegations made in a former employee’s lawsuit.

image.caption: John Cena, wrestler and actor.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s OK to love somebody when they’re not perfect’: how John Cena conquered Hollywood – and why he refuses to abandon Vince McMahon

segments.body: John Cena has moved from WWE stardom to a distinctive Hollywood career, often playing powerful men who are comfortable looking ridiculous. He describes his relationship with WWE as one of service and gratitude, and says the company has a legitimate share of ownership in the John Cena character he built there.

segments.title: An unresolved loyalty
segments.body: Cena says he feels no guilt or shame about his friendship with former WWE chairman Vince McMahon. McMahon resigned in 2024 after sexual-assault allegations and lawsuits, including a suit by former employee Janel Grant alleging assault and coercion. McMahon denies the allegations; the litigation was transferred to confidential private arbitration. Cena’s unwavering public support raises questions about the cost of his company loyalty.

content.headline: A Statement turns a failed climate meeting into absorbing human drama
content.shortHeadline: A Statement finds drama in a failed climate conference
content.standfirst: Tom McCarthy’s film draws much of its conference-room dialogue from the actual 1980 transcript, following experts as they struggle to agree on a response to climate change. Its ensemble drama makes the deadlock compelling without disguising the failure.

image.caption: A still from A Statement.

sources.originalTitle: A Statement review – outstanding climate change dramedy about a 1980 meeting

segments.body: In 1980, 20 experts met in Florida to advise Congress on climate change. A Statement recreates their marathon discussions, drawing the conference-room dialogue from the stenographer’s record. The group agreed on the underlying facts but never reached consensus or issued the requested statement.

segments.title: The people behind the debate
segments.body: The film’s strength, in the review’s view, is its ensemble: Paul Rudd moderates, Paul Giamatti brings wary pragmatism, and Evan Peters embodies urgency. The late-night conversations and personal reckonings beyond the official meeting give the historical debate emotional texture, while the failure to agree remains in plain sight.

content.headline: Paul Thomas Anderson’s Cameron Winter concert film captures a singular night
content.shortHeadline: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall is a concert film to savour
content.standfirst: Paul Thomas Anderson’s 35mm film preserves the spare performance and rapt audience that made Winter’s Carnegie Hall concert feel like a communion. It offers little to newcomers, but makes a striking document for listeners already drawn to his music.

image.caption: A still from Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall.

sources.originalTitle: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall review – Paul Thomas Anderson’s sumptuous recording is an immediate classic

segments.body: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall records the Geese frontman’s solo acoustic performance in a 75-minute film shot on 35mm. Paul Thomas Anderson was among the camera operators. The review praises the film’s rich colour and close attention to Winter’s voice, piano and the quiet of an audience focused on the music.

Anderson keeps the framing spare, largely letting the concert speak for itself. The result, the review argues, is a faithful record of a performance that felt less like a conventional show than a shared ritual. Its lack of interviews or explanatory material may limit its appeal beyond existing fans, but those who enter its world get a carefully made document of a defining night.

content.headline: After Blade stalled, Bassam Tariq and Mahershala Ali made a film of their own
content.shortHeadline: Bassam Tariq turned a stalled Blade project into a new film
content.standfirst: The director and Mahershala Ali brought ideas from the abandoned Marvel project into Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, a Houston-set thriller about faith, violence and fatherhood made on a more personal scale.

image.caption: Director Bassam Tariq at the Toronto Film Festival in September 2026.

sources.originalTitle: How Bassam Tariq pivoted from stalled Blade reboot to new Mahershala Ali thriller: ‘I’m happier I made this movie’

segments.body: Bassam Tariq says the collapse of his planned Blade reboot left him and Mahershala Ali with action sequences and ideas they could redirect into Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother. Ali plays a devout Muslim father who works as a contract killer, while Jon Cho’s pastor character leads a rival religious crusade in Tariq’s pulpy Houston-set thriller.

segments.title: A personal starting point
segments.body: The film’s story began in part with Tariq’s own panic after his wife developed an infection following the birth of their child. He searched New York for breast milk for his son, an experience that fed the film’s opening crisis. Tariq says the story became a way to explore faith and the importance of being present as a father.

content.headline: Digger divides critics over Tom Cruise’s audacious oil-tycoon satire
content.shortHeadline: Digger splits critics on Cruise’s oil-tycoon performance
content.standfirst: Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s eco-satire gives Cruise an extreme transformation as an oil baron facing a climate catastrophe. One review calls it laborious and glib; another embraces its eccentric scale and political bluntness.

image.caption: Tom Cruise as oil tycoon Digger Rockwell in Digger.

sources.originalTitle: Digger review – Tom Cruise’s loudmouth oil tycoon goes hard in Alejandro G Iñárritu’s eco-satire
Digger review: Tom Cruise takes the 'biggest risk of his career' in this 'love-it-or-hate-it' folly ★★★★☆

segments.body: In Digger, Tom Cruise plays a paunchy Texas oil tycoon whose drilling operation helps trigger a global crisis. The Guardian review finds striking images in the film but calls its satire shallow and laborious, arguing that the plot’s major turn undercuts the drama and leaves the tycoon’s claims about energy policy insufficiently challenged.

perspectives.body: The BBC review also sees an eccentric, divisive film, but finds its high-concept turns and outsize performance purposeful. It praises the satire’s political force and argues that Cruise’s willingness to take such an odd role is evidence against a straightforward Oscar-bait reading.

segments.title: A risky change of register
segments.body: Both reviews note the scale of Cruise’s transformation and the distance from his familiar action roles. They disagree on whether the film’s excess becomes empty self-indulgence or an engaging experiment: the Guardian is unconvinced, while the BBC critic says the gargantuan performance and environmental argument won them over despite stretches that could have been shorter.

content.headline: James Dean’s fragile talent outlasts the myth of the rebel
content.shortHeadline: James Dean beyond the rebel image
content.standfirst: A look back at East of Eden finds the actor’s most enduring quality not in his familiar image of cool defiance, but in a vulnerable performance shaped by his difficult relationship with his father and fear of fame.

image.caption: James Dean on the set of Giant in 1955.

sources.originalTitle: The truth about James Dean

segments.body: James Dean’s three starring roles made him an icon, but the profile argues that his performance in East of Eden is best understood through its vulnerability. Director Elia Kazan drew on Dean’s resentment towards his father when shaping Cal, the troubled son who cannot stop seeking his father’s approval.

segments.title: The moment that remains
segments.body: Dean died at 24, before the release of two of his star vehicles, and his death helped turn him into a symbol of living fast and dying young. The article returns instead to a scene in East of Eden where Cal embraces his father after his birthday gift is rejected: a raw, unscripted moment that reveals the desperate boy beneath the carefully preserved image.

content.headline: A new Sense and Sensibility makes Austen’s emotional balance feel current
content.shortHeadline: Sense and Sensibility still speaks to the social-media age
content.standfirst: Georgia Oakley’s darker adaptation of Jane Austen’s novel is uneven, but its sisters’ competing instincts resonate with modern pressures around privacy, romance and financial security.

image.caption: Daisy Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood in Sense and Sensibility.

sources.originalTitle: Every millennial should read Sense and Sensibility

segments.body: The new film follows sisters Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, whose contrasting responses to love and hardship give Jane Austen’s novel its title. The review finds Georgia Oakley’s adaptation uneven and gloomier than the 1995 film, but argues that the sisters’ struggle between restraint and romantic idealism remains recognisable.

segments.title: Heart, head and modern life
segments.body: The article connects Austen’s characters to a present-day tension: people are encouraged to share their feelings yet remain guarded in a world where private moments can be recorded and circulated. Marianne’s faith in a charming suitor obscures warning signs; Elinor’s restraint leaves her carrying grief alone. Austen’s question of how to live by feeling and judgement still travels.

content.headline: From Psycho to The Prestige: 15 films that land a great plot twist
content.shortHeadline: 15 film twists that still make audiences look twice
content.standfirst: This spoiler-aware guide revisits 15 memorable reversals, from Psycho’s early shock to later films that make viewers rethink the story they have been watching.

sources.originalTitle: The 15 best film plot twists of all time

segments.body: The list ranges across decades and genres, from Psycho and The Wicker Man to The Prestige, Parasite and M. Night Shyamalan’s The Sixth Sense. It foregrounds the turns themselves and how films use them to change the audience’s understanding of a character, a setting or the story’s rules.

The guide warns that spoilers are ahead. Its appeal is not simply the surprise, but the different ways a reveal can reframe what came before: a detective story becomes a character study, a family home turns uncanny, or a confident narrator proves unreliable.

content.headline: Friday Night Lights made small-town football a story about people
content.shortHeadline: Friday Night Lights found humanity beneath football’s glare
content.standfirst: Twenty years on, the drama’s handheld style, improvisational performances and close attention to Dillon, Texas, still distinguish it. Its football world is also one of pressure, inequality and hopes that do not always come true.

image.caption: Kyle Chandler and Connie Britton in Friday Night Lights.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Brave from the beginning’: 20 years of Friday Night Lights – the sports drama that dared to be different

segments.body: Friday Night Lights began with a high-school football town where a Friday game could shape the mood for days. The series drew on H.G. “Buzz” Bissinger’s reporting about Odessa, Texas, and carried forward its unease about racism, the pressure placed on young players and the resources football could draw away from schools.

segments.title: A different kind of realism
segments.body: Director Peter Berg encouraged improvisation and handheld camerawork, giving scenes a naturalism unusual for a network drama. Kyle Chandler and Connie Britton anchor the show as a coach and school counsellor trying to raise a family amid constant public scrutiny. Its five seasons also helped launch Jesse Plemons and Michael B. Jordan.

content.headline: Get Jiro turns food culture into a bloody satire of power
content.shortHeadline: Get Jiro serves food satire with a side of ultraviolence
content.standfirst: Anthony Bourdain’s graphic novel becomes an adult animation about chefs, crime and a future where food is the last pleasure that technology cannot virtualise. Its extravagant violence is part of a pointed joke about food’s status and power.

image.caption: Jiro, voiced by Brian Tee, in Get Jiro.

sources.originalTitle: Get Jiro: Anthony Bourdain’s ultraviolent sushi chef makes for wild, pulpy television

segments.body: In Get Jiro, food has become the last pleasure that a digital world cannot reproduce. In near-future Los Angeles, chefs wield the power of crime bosses and people will kill for restaurant reservations. The taciturn sushi chef Jiro is no innocent bystander: the opening scene makes clear how far the show will push its grotesque food jokes and violence.

The review finds the animation camp and knowingly excessive, with restaurant criticism and culinary jargon turned into street-level satire. Beneath the pulpy action, it sees an indictment of food as class currency, drawing on the graphic novel co-written by Anthony Bourdain, whose work joined kitchen machismo to empathy and curiosity about people.

content.headline: War turns a celebrity divorce into lavish, high-stakes television
content.shortHeadline: War makes a high-stakes game of divorce
content.standfirst: Sienna Miller and Dominic West lead George Kay’s glossy drama about a wealthy couple and the lawyers fighting over their separation. The review relishes its money, class conflict and escalating legal manoeuvres.

image.caption: James McArdle, Sienna Miller and Phoebe Fox in War.

sources.originalTitle: War review – Sienna Miller and Dominic West’s hellish divorce drama is massive, massive fun

segments.body: War centres on social-media mogul Morgan Henderson and actor Carla Duval, whose divorce becomes a public battle. Their legal teams—one established and old-fashioned, the other younger and more polished—look for leverage in their clients’ finances, reputations and relationships.

segments.title: Soap opera with legal briefs
segments.body: The review embraces the series as high-quality “balderdash”: a fast-moving tangle of prenups, betrayals, press tactics and double-crosses. Dominic West and Sienna Miller keep the central couple watchable without demanding sympathy, while Pip Torrens and a broad supporting cast give the legal shenanigans their own comic momentum.

content.headline: Richard E Grant’s Traitors blunder gives the celebrity series an early jolt
content.shortHeadline: Richard E Grant’s Traitors slip-up sets the series in motion
content.standfirst: The actor accidentally reveals his role almost as soon as he is chosen, creating a chaotic opening for the second celebrity series. The review argues that the misstep makes the game more compelling, not less.

image.caption: Richard E Grant and Maya Jama as the first hooded Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: Richard E Grant has already ruined The Celebrity Traitors. It’s brilliant

segments.body: After being chosen as a Traitor alongside Maya Jama, Richard E Grant tells Joe Lycett outright: “Oh, I’m a Traitor.” The review says the mistake was genuine, leaving Grant and Jama to manage the fallout while the Faithfuls try to work out why he would confess so quickly.

Rather than deflating the series, the blunder gives it a new source of suspense: Grant is delighted by the game, Jama tries to regain control, and the others are left guessing. The piece sees the show’s unpredictable personalities and high-camp atmosphere as the reason the format still feels fresh.

content.headline: Nigella Lawson brings a pleasure-first attitude to The Great British Bake Off
content.shortHeadline: Nigella brings pleasure, not guilt, to Bake Off
content.standfirst: The new judge’s delight in eating and refusal to call food “naughty” offer a welcome counterpoint to calorie-conscious food culture. A second review finds that her glamour also gives the familiar show a lift.

image.caption: Nigella Lawson on The Great British Bake Off.

sources.originalTitle: Nigella is dismantling skinny culture one ‘naughty cookie’ at a time
Nigella’s glamour saves Bake Off’s stale mix

segments.body: Nigella Lawson’s arrival as a Great British Bake Off judge has changed how the programme talks about food. She enjoys the bakes openly and objects when Paul Hollywood calls cookies “naughty”, saying people should take pleasure where they can. The review sees that response as a refreshing alternative to the pressure on women to monitor every bite.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s episode review also welcomes Lawson’s arrival, praising her confidence and sensual approach to baking as a boost to the familiar format. It notes that the show’s playful challenges remain, but argues her presence adds sophistication and star power.

segments.title: A different kind of judging
segments.body: Lawson’s approach contrasts with predecessor Prue Leith’s comments about whether a bake was worth the calories. The review argues that the contrast matters in a culture saturated with weight-loss messages: Bake Off becomes a mainstream space where a woman can enjoy rich food without apology or a calculation of how to compensate.

content.headline: Youth’s glamorous lead complicates its portrait of an ordinary middle-aged woman
content.shortHeadline: Youth asks who gets to look ordinary on television
content.standfirst: Sharon Horgan’s new comedy follows a 50-something woman juggling family, work and a changing body. The review praises the subject but questions whether a character framed as an everywoman can feel relatable when played by such a glamorous star.

image.caption: Sharon Horgan in Youth.

sources.originalTitle: Sharon Horgan’s Youth has one big problem

segments.body: Sharon Horgan created, wrote and stars in Youth as Alex, a literary agent dealing with a troubled teenage son, ageing parents, work pressures and changes to her body. The review sees value in a comedy about a woman in her fifties with a sex life, but argues that Horgan’s glamour can make the character feel remote from the “everywoman” the story intends.

segments.title: Who gets to be ordinary?
segments.body: The criticism is aimed less at Horgan than at television’s beauty standards. The piece argues that women are still expected to be exceptionally attractive to headline a show, even as stories give them more emotional complexity. It calls for the freedom to see women on screen as they are, rather than as an idealised version of themselves.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s future looks uncertain, but fans still believe it can return
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain future after its latest pause
content.standfirst: The BBC has ended its Disney+ partnership and cancelled a planned Christmas special, leaving the long-running series without a confirmed next chapter. Fans and writers disagree on why its recent revival faltered, but still want it back.

image.caption: Several actors who have played the Doctor, including Peter Capaldi, Jodie Whittaker and Ncuti Gatwa.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Since its latest series ended in 2025, Doctor Who has had no new episodes announced. The BBC has ended its collaboration with Disney+ and cancelled a planned Christmas special; it is seeking another partner to help fund future production. The series also has no current Doctor, and the BBC has declined to discuss the decision.

segments.title: A format built to change
segments.body: The article traces the show’s repeated reinventions, from its 2005 revival to a succession of Doctors and showrunners. Fans and former writers offer different explanations for the latest decline, including scripts and the shape of the Disney+ partnership. They agree that regeneration and renewal have always been central to the show—and that an archive alone is not enough for its most devoted viewers.

content.headline: The Split Up brings a British Asian family to a familiar legal drama
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up gives its legal drama a new British Asian family
content.standfirst: The spin-off moves the family-law format to Manchester and centres a predominantly British Asian cast and creative team. Its creators and stars discuss representation, family conflict and the freedom to build a new story.

image.caption: Ritu Arya in The Split Up.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: The Split Up follows Aria Kishan, a barrister expected to take over her father’s Manchester law firm, until her mother’s death disrupts the succession plan. As in The Split, high-stakes divorce cases run alongside fractures within the lawyers’ own family. The new series has a predominantly British Asian cast and creative team.

segments.title: Normal lives on screen
segments.body: Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted to create British Asian characters living ordinary lives rather than relying on familiar plots about terrorism or arranged marriage. Original-series creator Abi Morgan, now an executive producer, says the spin-off keeps the family drama’s emotional engine while giving a new writing team room to shape its own characters.

content.headline: Gears of War: E-Day’s excellent combat is trapped in repetitive design
content.shortHeadline: Gears of War: E-Day has great combat and too little else
content.standfirst: The prequel makes firefights feel weighty and fluid, but repetitive routes, scattered collectibles and awkward exploration blunt the impact of its alien invasion story.

image.caption: Marcus Fenix in Gears of War: E-Day.

sources.originalTitle: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring

segments.body: E-Day returns to the day the Locust emerged from underground, putting players with Marcus Fenix and a squad of soldiers amid the invasion. The review praises the combat: characters move more naturally, cover feels better integrated and destructible environments make firefights vivid and tactical.

The surrounding campaign does not keep pace. The squad repeatedly crosses familiar areas, open levels are crowded with collectibles and side objectives, and exploring can trigger a mission failure. The review finds that the game’s strongest ideas arrive early, leaving its excellent combat to carry a safe and repetitive experience.

content.headline: Resident Evil’s new film recreates the fear of playing the games
content.shortHeadline: Resident Evil’s film finds horror in the experience of play
